title: DHS Moves to Eliminate 60-Day Grace Period for H-1B Workers After Job Loss
excerpt: A proposed rule clearing White House review would strip the safety net that gives laid-off H-1B holders time to find new sponsors or leave the U.S.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has submitted a proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period that H-1B workers currently receive after losing their jobs.
  • The rule cleared White House Office of Management and Budget review but has not yet been published in the Federal Register for public comment.
  • If finalized, laid-off workers in H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, and other employment-based visa categories would lose their immigration status immediately upon termination.
  • The proposal is part of a broader wave of Trump administration actions targeting the H-1B program, including a proposed $103,265 fee for new hires.

The Department of Homeland Security has proposed eliminating the 60-day grace period that allows H-1B workers and other employment-based visa holders to remain in the United States after losing their jobs. The proposed rule, titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," was submitted to the Office of Management and Budget on August 6, 2026, and cleared review by August 28.

The rule has not yet been published in the Federal Register. Once published, it will undergo a public comment period of 30 to 60 days before DHS can finalize it. The current grace period remains in effect during the rulemaking process.

What the Grace Period Provides

Since January 2017, workers who lose their jobs while on H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, TN, E-1, E-2, and E-3 visas have been granted up to 60 days to find a new sponsoring employer, file a change of immigration status, or make arrangements to leave the country. The policy was introduced under a 2016 DHS regulation to give foreign workers a reasonable buffer after unexpected employment termination.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=nNqp7ciIzwM

In practice, the grace period has served as a critical safety net. USCIS has rarely shortened or denied it, according to immigration law firm Seyfarth Shaw, making it a reliable lifeline for foreign nationals navigating layoffs, corporate restructurings, or other employment disruptions.

"Eliminating the 60-day grace period is both inhumane and unworkable. People will not even have the time required to manage their leases, transition their children out of schools, or handle personal affairs."

— Ajay Jain Bhutoria, former White House adviser

Impact on Indian Workers and Families

The proposal would hit Indian nationals hardest. Indians account for roughly 72% of all H-1B visa holders, and the technology, consulting, and financial services sectors where they are concentrated have seen significant layoffs in recent years. Without the 60-day window, a layoff would immediately trigger an immigration crisis for the worker and their entire family.

Eligible dependents — spouses on H-4 visas and children — would also lose their status when the principal visa holder's employment ends. For families with children enrolled in American schools, mortgages, and established lives, the consequences would be severe.

Former White House adviser Ajay Jain Bhutoria has called for the grace period to be increased to 180 days rather than eliminated, arguing that even 60 days is often insufficient for highly skilled workers with families to arrange an orderly transition.

Part of a Broader Crackdown

The grace period proposal is one of several Trump administration actions targeting the H-1B program. Earlier in the same week, the administration proposed a $103,265 fee for new H-1B hires, according to Bloomberg Law. Combined with ongoing scrutiny of wage levels and specialty occupation definitions, the measures represent the most aggressive regulatory pressure on the program in years.

The proposal would effectively return the system to its pre-2017 framework, when job loss generally meant immediate loss of immigration status. Immigration attorneys warn this could accelerate a brain drain, pushing skilled workers toward countries like Canada, the UK, and Australia that offer more predictable pathways.

What Comes Next

The specific provisions of the rule will not be known until it is published in the Federal Register. Once published, affected workers, employers, and advocacy groups will have an opportunity to submit public comments. DHS could then modify, withdraw, or finalize the regulation based on the feedback received.

Immigration attorneys are advising H-1B holders to review their status, maintain valid documentation, and consult legal counsel about contingency plans. Workers currently in the grace period would likely be grandfathered under existing rules, but the timeline for finalization remains uncertain.
